title: Which checkout page won?
blurb: Version B wins on mobile AND wins on desktop — yet loses overall.
prompt: An AI product analyst reviewed an A/B test between checkout designs A and B. Find the two reasoning mistakes.

segments.label: Claim 1
segments.text: On mobile, Version B beat Version A (12% conversion vs 10%).

segments.label: Claim 2
segments.text: On desktop, Version B also beat Version A (32% conversion vs 30%).

segments.label: Claim 3
segments.text: However, due to a routing bug, 80% of A's visitors were on desktop while 80% of B's visitors were on mobile, giving overall averages of 26% for A and 16% for B.

segments.label: Claim 4
segments.text: Because Version A's combined conversion rate is 10 points higher (26% vs 16%), shipping Version A to all users will increase conversions.

segments.label: Claim 5
segments.text: In addition, Version A achieved 100% conversion in our VIP tier (2 purchases out of 2 visitors), proving VIP users strongly prefer A.

conclusion: Verdict: Ship Version A globally — it leads overall (26% vs 16%) and has 100% VIP conversion.

flaws.original: Version B actually wins on both mobile and desktop; A's higher combined average is a Simpson's paradox artifact of A getting far more high-converting desktop traffic.
flaws.corrupted: Because Version A's combined conversion rate is 10 points higher (26% vs 16%), shipping Version A to all users will increase conversions.

diagnosis_choices.label: Simpson's paradox: A only looks better overall because it got 80% desktop traffic, even though B beats A on every device.
You cannot compare conversion percentages between mobile and desktop users.
26% minus 16% is a 62.5-point gap, not a 10-point gap.
The overall average of 10% and 30% must always be 20% regardless of traffic split.

fix_choices.label: Compare within matched segments (or re-run with balanced randomization): B wins on both mobile and desktop, so B is better.
Ignore device type because total averages always override subgroup results.
Ship Version A on desktop and Version A on mobile to preserve the 26% overall rate.
Average the mobile and desktop rates of A and B without checking sample splits.

flaws.explanation: Desktop naturally converts ~3× higher than mobile. Giving Version A mostly desktop traffic inflates its pooled average even though Version B outperforms A on BOTH mobile (12% > 10%) and desktop (32% > 30%).
flaws.why_tempting: The headline combined number (26% vs 16%) feels more authoritative than subgroup breakdowns — until you look at the traffic weights.
flaws.catch_rule: When a pooled average contradicts every subgroup, check for imbalanced group weights (Simpson's paradox).
flaws.hint: Why did Version A average 26% overall when it lost on both mobile and desktop?

practice.problem: Hospital X has a higher survival rate than Hospital Y for both mild cases and severe cases, yet a lower overall survival rate. How is that possible?
practice.answer: Hospital X treats a much larger share of severe cases than Hospital Y.

flaws.original: With only 2 VIP visitors, 2/2 conversions is far too small a sample to draw any reliable conclusion about VIP preference.
flaws.corrupted: In addition, Version A achieved 100% conversion in our VIP tier (2 purchases out of 2 visitors), proving VIP users strongly prefer A.

diagnosis_choices.label: Tiny sample fallacy: 2 out of 2 visitors is just random noise and cannot prove VIPs prefer Version A.
100% conversion is mathematically impossible in an A/B test.
VIP users should never be included in checkout experiments.

fix_choices.label: Treat `n = 2` as inconclusive and collect a much larger randomized VIP sample before deciding.
Report it as 'nearly 100%' (95%) to look more conservative.
Drop one of the two VIP users to reduce variance.
Assume VIPs behave identically to mobile users instead of collecting data.

flaws.explanation: A headline '100%' hides a denominator of 2. Even a fair coin lands heads twice in a row 25% of the time — `n = 2` proves nothing.
flaws.why_tempting: Extreme percentages like '100%' grab attention and sound decisive when the tiny denominator is tucked in parentheses.
flaws.catch_rule: Whenever you see an eye-popping percentage ('100%', 'doubled!'), immediately check the raw count `n` behind it.
flaws.hint: Look at the numbers in parentheses in Claim 5.

practice.problem: A new café gets 5.0 stars from 2 reviews while an older café has 4.7 stars from 1,400 reviews. Why isn't 5.0 clearly better?
practice.answer: With only 2 reviews, the 5.0 average has huge uncertainty and could easily come from friends or luck.

clean_segments: On mobile, Version B beat Version A (12% vs 10%).
On desktop, Version B also beat Version A (32% vs 30%).
A routing bug sent 80% desktop traffic to A and 80% mobile traffic to B, distorting the pooled averages (26% vs 16%).
Because B wins within every device segment, the pooled lead for A is a Simpson's paradox artifact; we should fix randomization or favor B.
The VIP tier only had 2 visitors, which is far too small to draw any conclusion.
clean_conclusion: Version B outperforms A on both mobile and desktop; fix the traffic split rather than shipping A.
